planting.note: Plant rooted rhizome sections in spring into constantly moist to wet, strongly acidic, peaty soil in full sun to partial shade; small cranberry requires true bog conditions and will not thrive in ordinary garden soil.

directions: Plant in constantly moist to saturated, strongly acidic, peaty soil in full sun to partial shade, ideally in a lined bog bed amended heavily with peat moss; small cranberry is a circumboreal wild relative of the commercially grown large cranberry, with wiry, thread-like trailing stems, tiny evergreen leaves, and delicate pink, backward-swept flowers in early summer. It bears smaller, more strongly tart fruit than cultivated cranberry, ripening from late summer into fall and usable in the same jellies, sauces, and baked goods, though yields are lighter than commercial varieties. Because it is adapted to genuine sphagnum bog habitat, it needs sustained moisture and acidity that most garden soils cannot provide without significant modification, making a dedicated peat bog bed or large lined container the most realistic way to grow it outside its native cold, wet peatlands. Mulch with additional peat or pine needles each year to maintain acidity, and avoid any liming or alkaline amendments nearby.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring into well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; space generously, since Pennsylvania blackberry spreads by root sprouts into dense thickets if left unmanaged.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings in well-drained soil in full sun, spacing generously to accommodate rapid spread by root sprouts; Pennsylvania blackberry is one of the most common and widespread wild blackberries of the eastern United States, forming stout, heavily armed, upright to arching canes in old fields, fencerows, and forest edges. White flowers open in late spring, followed by large, firm, sweet-tart black drupes that ripen over a long midsummer season and are excellent fresh or in preserves. Its vigorous, thicket-forming habit makes it valuable for wildlife cover and erosion control on a bank or hedgerow but requires regular management (cutting root suckers or mowing a defined perimeter) in a maintained garden setting to prevent it from spreading beyond its intended space. After harvest, remove spent second-year floricanes at ground level to make room for the current season's new primocanes, which will fruit the following year.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring into well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Canadian blackberry is naturally nearly thornless, unlike most wild brambles, making it easier to harvest and maintain.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Canadian blackberry is an Appalachian and northeastern native distinguished from most wild brambles by canes that are nearly or entirely without prickles, making harvest and pruning far more pleasant than with typical thorny wild blackberries. White flowers in late spring give way to large, sweet, juicy black fruit ripening in mid- to late summer, well suited to fresh eating, baking, and preserves. It tolerates more shade than many fruiting brambles, performing well at woodland edges and in partially shaded hedgerows where full-sun brambles struggle. Manage its spread by root suckers with an annual perimeter mowing or trenching, and remove spent floricanes after harvest each year to keep the patch productive and open.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown shrubs in spring into very well-drained, dry, rocky or gravelly, alkaline soil in full sun; red barberry is a spiny, evergreen Southwestern native adapted to arid canyon and mountain slope conditions.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, dry, rocky soil in full sun; red barberry is a dense, spiny-leaved evergreen shrub of the desert Southwest, its holly-like, blue-gray foliage giving way in spring to small, fragrant, bright yellow flower clusters that draw bees. Clusters of tart, juicy red berries follow in summer, edible fresh in small quantities and traditionally used to make jelly, syrup, and a tart, refreshing beverage similar to that made from the related algerita (Berberis trifoliolata). The dense, thorny branching makes it a useful barrier or wildlife hedge planting, offering cover and food for birds while deterring foot traffic. It is extremely drought and heat tolerant once established and requires minimal care beyond occasional shaping, needing supplemental water only during the driest extended stretches.

planting.note: Sow fresh seed in fall so winter cold breaks dormancy naturally, into well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; American barberry is the native, non-invasive Appalachian counterpart to the widely planted but ecologically problematic Japanese barberry.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; American barberry is a thorny, deciduous Appalachian native shrub with small, spine-tipped leaves, drooping clusters of small yellow flowers in late spring, and bright red, elongated berries that ripen in fall and persist into winter, providing food for birds when little else is available. It is a genuinely native, non-invasive alternative for gardeners who want the ornamental berry and thorny-hedge qualities of barberry without planting the widely naturalized and ecologically disruptive Japanese barberry. Because Berberis species can serve as an alternate host for wheat stem rust, avoid planting it in large numbers near commercial grain fields, a precaution that led to historic eradication programs targeting common barberry in agricultural regions. Otherwise easy to grow and largely trouble-free, it works well as an informal barrier hedge, wildlife planting, or specimen in a naturalistic border.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in early spring into very well-drained, dry, rocky or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; wax currant is a drought-tolerant Rocky Mountain and Great Basin native adapted to dry, rocky foothill and canyon slopes.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, dry, rocky soil in full sun to partial shade; wax currant is a compact, twiggy shrub with small, rounded, waxy-textured leaves and tubular, pale pink to whitish spring flowers that are visited by early-season bees and occasional hummingbirds. Small, bright red, glossy berries ripen in summer and are edible, though quite tart and seedy, generally best used cooked into jelly or syrup rather than eaten fresh out of hand. It is markedly more drought tolerant than most cultivated currants and gooseberries, thriving in the same dry, rocky, low-fertility soils found on sagebrush foothills and canyon slopes throughout its native range. Prune out the oldest stems periodically to renew productive wood, and avoid rich soil or frequent irrigation, both of which encourage lush, mildew-prone growth in this otherwise tough, low-maintenance native shrub.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in early spring into consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; swamp black currant is a cold-climate North American native of streambanks, swamp margins, and moist forest understory.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; swamp black currant is a densely bristled, thorny shrub native to cool, moist forests, streambanks, and swamp edges across northern North America and the Rocky Mountains. Small, saucer-shaped, maroon to pinkish flowers dangle in spring, followed by dark purple-black, glandular-bristled berries that are edible but have a musky, somewhat unpleasant raw flavor most foragers find best transformed into jelly or syrup with enough sugar to balance it. The fine, sharp prickles covering the stems make careful handling and gloves worthwhile at pruning and harvest time. It fills a valuable niche for shaded, consistently moist planting sites too wet or shady for most other fruiting shrubs, and is a useful streambank or rain garden edge planting where the goal is habitat and food value as much as fruit quality.
sources: University of Alaska Fairbanks Cooperative Extension
